article_text:
An ancient fragment of a statue of a Roman emperor sold last night at Sotheby’s for $34.3 million, a sum that the house has deemed an auction record for a Roman antiquity.

The three-and-a-half-foot-tall marble fragment depicts only the emperor’s torso, adorned in an elegant bronze cuirass. According to Sotheby’s, it once belonged to a larger statue of an emperor from the Julio-Claudinian dynasty and dates to the 1st century CE. Like many Roman statues, it is a copy of a Greek one.

The statue is thought to have come from Dalmatia, per a provenance supplied by Sotheby’s, which last sold the work in 2010 to an Austrian collector. That year, the statue sold for $7.36 million, which means that it has more than quadrupled in value in the last decade and a half.

This time around, Sotheby’s gave the work an $8 million–$12 million estimate. When it appeared at a New York auction called “Magnum Opus” on Wednesday night, the piece ended up generating a 14-minute bidding war. (That battle was, in some ways, for show: The statue was guaranteed and had more than one irrevocable bid, meaning that it was assured to sell, even before it hit the block.) With premium fees accounted for, the statue sold for nearly triple its high estimate.

“The sculpture embodies the cross-category vision at the heart of this collection: a work whose historical importance, rarity and aesthetic power transcend traditional collecting boundaries,” Alexandra Olsman, Sotheby’s vice president and antiquities specialist, said in a statement. “Few ancient marbles combine such remarkable preservation, scholarly significance and visual impact, and tonight’s result reflects the enduring appeal of truly exceptional objects.”

The work has an unusual history. For years, it resided in the holdings of the heirs to Wilhelm Aloys Maximilian Neumann, a 19th-century collector based in Graz, Austria. At the end of World War II, with the Soviet troops having advanced into Austria, the family hid away the sculpture in an area between two doors, then plastered over the portals. It took a redesign of the Neumann family’s home for the sculpture to emerge anew, per a 2010 New York Times report .

Back then, one Sotheby’s official thought it was worth no more than $900,000 before investigating further, the Times reported.

Sotheby’s did not release the past record for an ancient Roman antiquity, but at least one result from the past two decades approaches the sum brought in by the marble torso. In 2007, a 2,000-year-old bronze statue of Artemis came to auction, also at Sotheby’s, where it sold for $28.6 million , more than four times what the house said it expected. The British dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi bought it at the time.

Wednesday’s “Magnum Opus” sale was composed entirely of works from one mysterious individual’s collection. They are part of a grouping of 600 objects from those holdings that are due to come to auction this week at Sotheby’s, with more to follow at sales staged in New York and Paris through 2027.

The Roman torso statue accounted for more than half of last night’s $63 million haul. That sum, which includes buyer’s premium, outpaces Sotheby’s presale estimate for all three of this week’s auctions, which it said were expected to bring in $60 million when they were announced over the summer.

Also sold last night were significant paintings by Canaletto, Luis Meléndez, and Jacob van Ruisdael, though none set records. There were also an ancient Roman head of a girl and a fragment of a Safavid carpet that sold for $2.5 million and $448,000, respectively.

article_text:
H ere for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Christmas Eve by the appearance of three Christmas ghosts, from yuletides past, present and future. It sticks to the accepted narrative beats and more or less all the familiar episodes, but with a few twists.

There is a witty and ingenious new prologue sequence in which Scrooge’s equally grumpy partner Jacob Marley, played by Ian McKellen, is still alive, going into a full Stadler-and-Waldorf double-act with his old colleague. (Wait – did The Muppet Christmas Carol inspire this ?) And West shows us his scary-movie style by having that scene coming to a disturbing close with a kettle’s eerie whistle as it comes to the boil.

As well as pointedly asking about prisons and workhouses, Scrooge now actually accuses the charitable gentlemen of stealing the donations themselves, and there’s a terrible new end in store for cheerful Mr Fezziwig, which the film suggests is what finally embittered Scrooge against the undeserving poor. His lost love Belle is here a novelist, an idea borrowed from romance author Michelle Griep. Andrea Riseborough , Tramell Tillman and Robert Strange play the three ghosts; Rupert Grint is his pinch-faced clerk Bob Cratchit, and Sam Claflin is his cheerful nephew Fred, son of his once adored sister Fanny.

As Scrooge himself, Depp is in fact rather good; theatrically bad-tempered and petulant and, as with his Jack Sparrow, I suspect Depp’s comedy timing and sonorous British accent might have been learned from his old Fast Show comrade Paul Whitehouse. He is better at the unredeemed Scrooge than the saved version at the end, where some of the abject pathos is missing.

This is a decent enough new version, avoiding any big new revisionist takes which might have clunked, though perhaps Dickens himself might not have agreed with the church scene and the solemn use of Silent Night to accompany the Christmas-everywhere montage. He might have pictured something more secular.

article_text:
“Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.”

At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film was Chicken Shop Date , which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.

Now that we have established I am not in fact Amelia Dimoldenberg – and that any boning today will be strictly chicken-related – Ali changes tack. Whenever anyone comes near our table, he loudly explains, to my embarrassment, that we are actually conducting a major drug deal. Having seemingly worked his way through the entire menu, he starts asking what else he would need to buy to get the bill up to £500, after discovering that the Guardian is footing it.

It is, in other words, reassuringly easy to tell that not everything about Ali G has changed, even though a lot has happened in the “20 decades” (he means 24 years) since he was last on the big screen in Ali G Indahouse. In that time, the UK has had nine prime ministers, survived a global pandemic and seen the rise of #MeToo and Black Lives Matter. Or, as Ali puts it rather more succinctly in the trailer: “The world went to crap: there was Covid, wars and Ed Sheeran”.

Now he’s back in Ali G: Who Iz I? – and, inevitably, not everybody is delighted. The trailer alone has prompted accusations that the fake dreadlocks, Rastafarian imagery and faux-Jamaican persona now look less like satire and more like an outdated racial caricature. Which is how, 24 years after Ali G first took his home town of Staines global, I find myself sitting opposite him in his old manor, trying to work out whether the UK is ready to show him some respect again.

Parked outside is the same yellow Renault 5 I remember from Indahouse, now with a homemade Uber sign stuck in the windscreen. Around his neck hangs a diamond teddy bear clutching two sacks of money. It “used to be part of the crown jewels and was worn by the queen, RIP. A bloke who worked as a dog washer at Windsor palace nicked it and then came into the Crooked Billet pub in Iver Heath, where me bought it off him for 20K when me was rich,” he claims.

More bafflingly, he is wearing four watches. “Dem are for different time zones – dis one is Staines, dis one is Egham, dis one iz Langley Village and dis one iz Scrotland.” There is plenty more to take in, but I should probably attempt to conduct the interview I actually came here for.

So how should I address you – Ali, Ali G or Mr G? Me iz known by me mates as “De G”, “G-Dog” and “De Ali-torney G-eneral” … and by Staines Benefits Office as Richard Watkins, Kelvin Matthews and Priyanka Patel.

And what happened to the dreads? Me ain’t never had dreads. Me wears the Rasta bonnet because – and me iz trusting you to keep dis secret – dat’s where me keeps me stash, the ganja. Perfect place because the cops ain’t allowed to look under it for religious reasons, innit.

We find out in the trailer that you’re about to become a dad. How are you preparing? Are you and your Julie going to NCT classes? Me has actually already become a daddy, something dat for the last 40 years me has prepared for five times every day. Me usually just prepared with me Julie, although one time we also prepared with Cheryl from Abrakebabra in dis marble Jacuzzi me bought off eBay, which tragically didn’t end well. Me put it upstairs at Nan’s house, when me filled it with water and the three of us got in, it was too heavy and broke through the floor and landed on me Nan, who was sitting in the room downstairs. Luckily it killed her instantly, completely squashed her. She died happy because just one week before, me had bought her a new pair of double-F swingaz for her 88th birthday. The weight of the Jacuzzi caused them to literally explode; one of her nipples was found three streets away. Anyway, when one life ends, another one starts, and me iz loving being a dad.

What sort of dad are you? There have been some discipline issues. No matter how many times me tells the baby, “Hands off, dem iz mine!”, him keeps trying to grab me Julie’s swingaz. But there you go – like his dad, he iz a boobs man, innit. Me loves him and he iz well brainy, at six months old him can already read audiobooks.

Staines officially became Staines-upon-Thames in 2012 , partly to improve the town’s image after years of association with you – but now there’s a petition calling for a statue of you in the town. Do you feel vindicated? And if they build it, would you pose for it – perhaps naked, like Michelangelo’s David? Firstly, it ain’t because of me they changed the name of Staines. It’s because in 2012 the River Thames started flowing through the town, so they added it to the name, innit. Thirdly, me iz well proud dat they want to put a statute of me in the middle of Staines. Me Julie says the only difference between dat and the real thing iz dat the statute won’t be selling ganja – they’ll both be hanging around the town centre doing nothing, ha ha ha! Unfortunately, as well as loads of people wanting the statute, there are also loads of people who don’t, because of racialism. Me ain’t gonna let them win and iz willing to pay out of me Julie’s pocket for an Ali G erection in the middle of Staines.

after newsletter promotion

This is your first film in 24 years. Why come back now? Did the world need Ali G, or did Ali G need the world? Dis ain’t actually me first film in 24 years. Me has also made about 300 others with me Julie and iz hoping Amazon will buy them off me and put them in the “members only” part of their site. But to answer your question, the world needed me. Dis movie will be the most important release since the Jeffrey Einstein files, and me made it to increase the peace, bring both sides together and hopefully prevent world war two from ever happening. It has also got more boning in it than the Einstein files – all of it legal – and because me iz now woke, me also included a nude man’s battyhole to keep the LGBLT community happy.

The Guardian has already been arguing about whether you should have come back at all. Arwa Mahdawi wrote “Ali G is back. I really wish he wasn’t”, while Jason Okundaye argued that Britain – and the joke – have changed. Jacob Rees-Mogg , meanwhile, has defended you on his Instagram, describing you as “clever, satiric humour that makes the country look faintly foolish. And that’s no bad thing.” So who understands Ali G better in 2026: the Guardian or Jacob Rees-Mogg? Me ain’t never heard of any of those people, but from their names it seems to me dat Jacob Rees-Mogg iz the only person of colour, so him supporting me iz all dat matters. There are always gonna be haterz, innit. Me ain’t the first intellectual to get dat – it happened to Jesus, it happened to Gandhi, it even happened to Brooklyn Beckham. For the good of humanoidkind, me has just got to keep speaking out. People shutting me down ain’t nothing new. In fact, me was cancelled just two years ago by Staines Benefits Office for pretending to be a disabled Albanian woman with seven children. Me just bounced right back with a new name. Don’t never let the authorities oppress you, innit.

You’ve come back to a world full of influencers, pranksters, podcasters and people asking strangers stupid questions on TikTok. Do you feel like everyone’s basically nicked your act? For real, loads of people have been copying me, especially the way me looks and talks – which makes them cultural appropriators and dat iz well out of order. It makes me well sad how fick the world has become since me was on telly doing interviews 20 decades ago – most reporters now can’t even correctly spell the word “jourmalist”, let alone ask brainy questions like you and me does do, innit.

You’ve spent your career interviewing politicians, experts and other important people. Who would you most like to interview now? Me has always dreamed big, both in me personal life – for example, last night me imagined doing it with Sydney Sweeney; dat iz a woman, by the way, in case you ain’t heard of her. Me ain’t got nothing against homosapiens, me just ain’t one of them – and also in me professional life. Check dis: me wants to do the biggest interview ever – to go up to heaven and have a chat with none other than God himself. Me’d have a look around heaven – iz it any good, or iz it well boring, just a load of old blokes sitting around playing harps? Then me’d have a puff with God and ask him the tough questions: why does him allow terrible things to happen to the Earth, like wars, diseases and Coldplay? Also, while me was up there, me’d check in on me Nan, see if she’s doing all right and if she can still remember the Netflix password for our house.

Who is the stupidest person you’ve ever interviewed? The most fickest person me ever spoke to was Domald Trump. How him ever became America’s prime minister me will never know. Also, how did him get to marry all them really fit women – first Ivanka, then Stormy Daniels and now dat one who looks like a Transformer, Melania?

By now Ali has eaten an alarming amount of chicken. I’ve laughed far more than I expected to – including a few times when I probably shouldn’t. He is still crude, badly informed and completely inappropriate. But that was always the trick: every so often, the stupidest person in the room accidentally asks the smartest question. Before we go our separate ways, there’s just one question I need to ask. Does he think I’ve got what it takes to join the West Staines Massiv? Is there some kind of initiation process?

“Me’ll have to check with the rest of me posse first – his name iz Dangerous Dave,” says Ali. “Me’ll ask him when he finishes work at HSBC at 5pm.”

Ali G: Who Iz I? is in cinemas from 23 October.

Sacha Baron Cohen

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "What does one come looking for at a photography fair? article_text:
What does one come looking for at a photography fair? Cameras to weigh in the hand, lenses to screw on, test counters where you can switch from one to the other. And photographers explaining how they use them. That is Sigma’s usual wager, and it sets up a Rencontres space at the heart of the Salon, from October 8 to 11. From Friday October 9 to Sunday October 11, presentations and discussions “around the practice of the image” follow one another.

In this space, professionals, in photography and in video, detail their methods and their equipment choices, and the Japanese manufacturer takes the opportunity to show how they “select and use” its lenses. Sigma says the sessions are aimed at “all kinds of users”. The programme runs to a dozen 45-minute sessions, except for one shorter interlude devoted to aviation enthusiasts.

From wide-angle to telephoto

Friday October 9 opens at 11 a.m. with the Sigma France team, who present the new 2026 products and, according to the brand, hand over “all the keys” to plan a visit. “An ideal introduction”, it announces, with the obligatory exclamation mark. At 12:30 p.m., Nadia Vialan, creator of the blogs “Blog Photo Lumix” and “Partons en voyage” (“Let’s Travel”), runs through the Art, Contemporary and Sports lines, from ultra-wide-angle for urban exploration to telephoto for nature photography. A tour of the catalogue to work out which prime or which zoom suits which project.

At 2 p.m., the Fondation des Œuvres Sociales de l’Air (FOSA) takes the microphone for 20 minutes. A Sigma partner for ten years, it hands out, on the Rencontres space, the prizes of a contest reserved for spotters, aviation enthusiasts who watch for planes the way others watch for birds. The grand winner leaves with a Sigma lens, in keeping with a ten-year-old partnership.

Long lenses then fill the afternoon, and the 300-600mm F4 DG OS | Sports takes the lead. At 2:30 p.m., Marc Schoeffel, photographer and videographer, has been observing Alsatian wildlife for several years, birds in particular. Creator of a widely followed YouTube channel, he has built solid day-to-day experience with long focal lengths and was one of the first to test this zoom for mirrorless cameras. At 4 p.m., Olivier and Frédéric Larrey, brothers and professional photographers, take over, from Norway to Japan. On their Leica SL3 bodies, they alternate between the 200mm F2 and the 500mm F5.6, prized for their compactness when travelling, and bring out the 300-600mm for their most ambitious projects.

Ultra-bright

Saturday October 10 changes focal length and light. At 11 a.m., Lou Sonsino, a photographer based in Lille, explains her method for portraiture and family photography: intimate moments, from pregnancy to birth, documented with kindness and exclusively in natural light. Her tool, the 50mm F1.2 DG | Art, lets her do without artificial lighting, even when light is scarce. She also promises to share her way of talking with her subject to achieve a “soft and authentic” look.

At 12:30 p.m., Gardères & Dohmen take up a challenge set by Sigma. This duo, regular speakers at the space and used to professional assignments, from corporate to weddings, set aside their usual equipment to test the APS-C Contemporary range on personal and family subjects. They deliver their feedback on these compact zooms, with the idea of photographing “naturally and discreetly”.

At 2:30 p.m., Tony Noël, a Lyon-based photographer and regular collaborator of Sigma France, presents the 85mm F1.2 DG | Art, unveiled to the public for the first time at the Salon. Chosen to make the images for the international launch campaign, he describes his first shoots in the field and what this “ultra-bright” lens brings to portraiture. This is the session that doubles as a preview.

The day closes at 4 p.m. with cinema. Laurent B, Cine Specialist at Sigma France, presents the AF Cine Line range, which combines the ergonomics and design of traditional cinema lenses with the advantages of autofocus. Videographers Thibault Loosveldt and Arnaud Moro join him to recount their latest shoots with the 28-45mm T2 FF and the 28-105mm T3 FF. An odd one out at a photography fair? Let us recall that the event is called, precisely, Salon Photo & Vidéo.

Travelling light

We hit the road on Sunday October 11. At 11 a.m., William Chareyre, a Lyon-based photographer, recounts a trip through Southeast Asia undertaken with a precise constraint: limiting the weight and bulk of his equipment. He explains why he chose the primes and zooms of the Contemporary range to travel across Vietnam, and how this compact kit let him adapt to every reporting situation. The payoff is a practical exchange on putting together “a camera bag optimised for travel”.

At 12:30 p.m., a change of scenery with Lolita Charlet, a Lille-based portrait and fashion photographer. Her colourful world, inspired by the sixties and seventies, gives a central place to sets, styling and accessories. She presents her creative approach and her shooting with the 17-40mm F1.8 DC | Art mounted on a Fujifilm body, which allows her to produce most of her work, then her methods for building a project and her advice for directing a model with ease.

At 2:30 p.m., Marie Bouhiron looks back on her round-the-world trip, which began with a “simple objective”: to document the planet and meet the cultures that inhabit it. The word is Sigma’s, and it lands neatly in this context. She draws on a selection of her most striking images, made with a travel kit of Sigma lenses, and shares anecdotes and equipment choices.

This programme is therefore an in-house affair: each session is tied to a lens or a range, and the whole reads like a catalogue told in the first person. And the line-up has plenty to hold the attention. The camera bodies vary (Leica SL3 for the Larrey brothers, Fujifilm for Lolita Charlet), so do the genres, from wildlife reportage to fashion, and the questions are about the craft: how to direct a model, how to pack a bag, how to talk to a subject. What remains, between two talks, is to check the promises on one’s own camera, at the test counters.

The Sigma space can be visited at the Salon Photo & Vidéo, October 8 to 11, 2026, at the Grande Halle de la Villette, Paris. Full programme (in French): Salon Photo & Vidéo 2026 : le programme des Rencontres Sigma . Sigma France is offering invitations with the code SIGMA26 on the Salon ticket office .
